query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy is a solid refrigeration working medium that exhibits a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor load-bearing integrity and tends to crack. What single intervention could increase its integrity while preserving caloric performance in these operating regimes? State one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, predicted integrity and caloric outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, applicable field, pressure, temperature, and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small fraction (1–3 at.%) of titanium (Ti) as an alloying element into the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy will increase its load-bearing integrity (fracture toughness and resistance to cracking) without significantly degrading its caloric response under applied magnetic field and pressure-field operation.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy, as-cast or annealed, exhibiting large caloric effects but poor mechanical integrity.
generation.intervention: Add 1–3 atomic percent Ti to the alloy composition, forming (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38Ti_x (x = 0.01–0.03).
generation.conditions: Applied magnetic fields up to 2 T, hydrostatic pressures up to 1 GPa, temperatures between 250–350 K, mechanical loading up to the yield point.
generation.structural_mediator: Ti addition is expected to promote grain boundary strengthening and reduce intergranular cracking by forming a more ductile matrix or by refining grain size.
generation.mechanism: Ti acts as a grain boundary strengthener and may promote solid solution strengthening, reducing stress concentration at grain boundaries and inhibiting crack propagation, while not interfering with the magnetostructural transition responsible for the caloric effect.
generation.predicted_outcome: Fracture toughness and resistance to cracking will increase by at least 30% compared to the baseline alloy, while the caloric response (ΔS, ΔT under field/pressure) will decrease by less than 10%.
generation.baseline: Original (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy without Ti, exhibiting large caloric effects but poor mechanical integrity.
generation.boundary: Effect is expected for Ti additions in the 1–3 at.% range; higher Ti content may degrade caloric performance. Valid for operation under fields ≤2 T, pressures ≤1 GPa, temperatures 250–350 K.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty exists regarding the precise impact of Ti on the magnetostructural transition; excessive Ti may suppress the caloric effect. The optimal Ti content must be experimentally determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 (control) and (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38Ti_0.02 (intervention). Subject both to mechanical testing (fracture toughness, crack propagation under load), and measure caloric response (ΔS, ΔT) under applied magnetic field and pressure at 300 K.
measurements: Caloric effect (ΔS, ΔT) under field and pressure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If Ti addition does not increase fracture toughness by at least 30% or if caloric response decreases by more than 10% compared to the control, the hypothesis is falsified.
